title: Feel the Fear and Do It Anyway

facts.claim: The chapter opens: 'Are you a victim, or are you taking responsibility for your life?' Jeffers says many people think they take responsibility when they do not; the victim mentality is subtle and takes many forms.

Example Edward: a wealthy high-powered executive in constant anxiety; when Jeffers suggested professional help he said everything would be fine if his wife were more loving, his boss stopped leaning on him and his son stopped taking drugs.
Example Mara: great job, lovely apartment, many friends; continual complaint about her ex-husband who never pays child support, and a son accusing her of being selfish.

Jeffers writes that you are consciously or unconsciously 'choosing' to be in that lousy job, choosing to stay in a destructive relationship, etc.; if you can create your own misery you can also create your own joy.

Jeffers explicitly does not ask the reader to believe they are responsible for all experiences in life; she asks them to believe they are the cause of their reactions to everything that happens to them.
She gives seven definitions of taking responsibility; the first: never blaming anyone else for anything you are being, doing, having or feeling. The second: not blaming yourself.

Jeffers describes her own past: hours on the phone with girlfriends complaining about the men in her life ('one was always late, one was incredibly stingy...'); she calls it a 'Moan and Groan Society'; the payoff was not having to create her own happiness.
Now when angry at her husband she asks herself: 'What am I not doing in my life that I could be doing that I am blaming him for not doing for me?'

Case Jean: stuck in a job she hated, playing the 'if only' game (if only the job market were better, if only she had better skills). Her payoffs: no risk of rejection in a job search, the job was easy and she knew she could handle it, no extra energy needed, relatively secure.
Once Jean saw her payoffs she had at least three choices: stay and be miserable, stay and choose to enjoy the job, or choose to find a more satisfying job. She broke away and found a new job.
Jeffers says payoffs are not hard to find once you know they exist: sit down with pencil and paper and list them; if you cannot find them, ask a friend.
Pain-to-Power vocabulary: 'I can't' to 'I won't', 'I should' to 'I could', 'It's not my fault' to 'I'm totally responsible', 'If only' to 'Next time'.

rejected.claim: Exercise: write 'Bunu ben seçtim' under every complaint (old text's three-line rewrite list as a formal exercise)
rejected.reason: The book states the 'you are choosing to' framing in prose and recommends listing payoffs; a written 'I chose this' exercise under each complaint is not verified in that form.

rejected.claim: 'As your attitude changes, circumstances start changing too'
rejected.reason: Not found as a book claim; promise-like generalisation.

rejected.claim: 'Taking responsibility is not taking blame, it is taking back power' as a quote
rejected.reason: Idea matches definition 2 (not blaming yourself) but the wording is not a book quote.

1257.note: Center (victim vs choosing, responsibility as not blaming) verified in full text; rebuilt around Jean's payoffs and Edward. Unverified 'write I chose this' exercise dropped.
